value.overview: The Yellow-billed Cacique is a medium-sized tropical songbird of the blackbird family. It has entirely black plumage contrasted by a yellow to yellow-orange bill and a yellow or orange-yellow eye. Unlike many caciques, it is usually secretive and closely associated with dense vegetation, especially bamboo, Heliconia thickets, marsh edges, and streamside growth. Its range extends from southern Mexico through Central America to northern South America, including much of the Caribbean slope of Costa Rica.
value.classification: The Yellow-billed Cacique belongs to the family Icteridae, which includes blackbirds, orioles, grackles, and other caciques. It is the only species in the genus Amblycercus.
value.identification: Adults are about 23 centimeters long and appear almost completely glossy black. The bill is distinctive: fairly long, narrow, and yellow or yellowish with a darker or grayish culmen. The eye is yellow to yellow-orange, while the legs and feet are dark gray. It is generally recognized by its combination of all-black body, bright bill, and preference for moving through dense cover. Its calls include varied whistles, churring notes, and other vocalizations given from concealed vegetation.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from southern Mexico through Central America, extending south through Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, and northwestern Venezuela. In Costa Rica it is mainly associated with the northern lowlands and the Caribbean slope, where it may occur from near sea level into foothill areas; local records also show it at higher elevations. Typical habitats include wet lowland forest, young secondary growth, stream and river margins, marshy ground, bamboo stands, Heliconia thickets, and other dense vegetation. It often favors damp, tangled cover rather than open woodland.
value.migrationStatus: The Yellow-billed Cacique is generally a resident species in Costa Rica and is not considered a regular long-distance migrant there. Individuals may move locally in response to food, water, or habitat conditions, but Costa Rican birds are present throughout the year.
value.breeding: Breeding in Costa Rica is reported mainly from January through June. The species is seasonally monogamous, with pairs defending nesting territories in dense vegetation. In lowland Central America, nests are commonly placed within thick bamboo or similarly tangled thickets, which provide concealment from predators. Clutches contain about one to five eggs. The female performs most incubation and feeding, while both adults protect and provision the young. Pairs may use coordinated calls while maintaining contact near the nest.
value.dietFeeding: Yellow-billed Caciques are omnivorous, taking many insects and other small invertebrates as well as fruit. They search methodically through dense foliage and tangled stems, and their narrow, strong bills can be used to probe bark, plant stalks, and seed pods. Reported foods include insects, spiders, and fruits, including pods of Inga trees. Their feeding also contributes to seed dispersal in the forests and thickets where they live.
value.behavior: This cacique is more often heard than seen because it spends much of its time inside dense bamboo, Heliconia, shrubbery, or streamside vegetation. It usually forages at low or middle levels and moves deliberately through cover while inspecting leaves and stems. Pairs may remain together and defend a territory, especially during breeding. Vocal communication includes whistles, churring sounds, and sharper warning notes. When disturbed, it commonly slips away through vegetation instead of flying into open areas.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not considered to be undergoing a rapid decline, although detailed population estimates are limited and local trends may differ.
